DOCUMENT:
Vendor Comparison: Standard Parcel Delivery Contract
Larkspur Home, Operations, June 2026

1. Purpose
Our contract with our current standard-delivery carrier ends on 30 September 2026. This paper compares three shortlisted carriers and recommends which should carry our standard (two-to-four-day) parcels from October.

2. Volumes and requirements
We dispatch an average of 42,000 standard parcels a month: about 70% weigh under 2 kg (cushions, textiles, small homeware) and 30% weigh 2 to 10 kg (lamps, mirrors, small furniture). Our requirements are on-time delivery of at least 95%, a damage rate below 0.5%, full tracking, and a returns service.

Damage and loss matter to us commercially. Each damaged or lost parcel costs us on average £48 in replacement stock, return shipping and customer service time, and damaged items are the most common cause of one-star reviews.

3. Trial
Between 1 April and 31 May 2026, each shortlisted carrier delivered a share of our orders, allocated at random by the warehouse management system, about 5,000 parcels per carrier. We measured on-time delivery against the promised date, damage reported by customers within 14 days, and lost parcels.

Table 1. Prices and trial performance
Carrier | Price, under 2 kg | Price, 2-10 kg | On-time delivery | Damage rate | Lost per 10,000 parcels
SwiftDrop | £3.10 | £4.60 | 96.2% | 0.4% | 3
ParcelLine | £2.85 | £4.95 | 93.1% | 0.9% | 8
Meridian | £3.30 | £4.40 | 97.5% | 0.3% | 2

On-time delivery was above 95% for all three carriers during the trial, and all three offer full tracking and a returns service.

4. Cost comparison
Applying our 70/30 weight mix, the average cost per parcel is £3.55 for SwiftDrop, £3.48 for ParcelLine and £3.63 for Meridian. On 42,000 parcels a month, the monthly cost would be £149,100 for SwiftDrop, £146,160 for ParcelLine and £152,460 for Meridian. ParcelLine is therefore the cheapest option, saving £2,940 a month against SwiftDrop and £6,300 a month against Meridian, or between about £35,000 and £76,000 a year.

5. Customer contact
"Where is my order?" contacts are our largest single category of customer service enquiry. During the trial, ParcelLine deliveries generated 6 such contacts per 1,000 parcels, compared with 11 for SwiftDrop and 10 for Meridian. ParcelLine's live-tracking app clearly reduces customer contacts, and at an average handling cost of £3.20 per contact this would save about £670 a month at our volumes. From 1 May, ParcelLine parcels also carried our new proactive delivery-day text message, which we were testing on one carrier before rolling it out.

6. Other considerations
All three carriers can collect from our warehouse daily at 6 pm. ParcelLine and SwiftDrop offer a 12-month contract; Meridian requires 24 months. SwiftDrop and Meridian have both handled our peak-season volumes for other retailers of similar size, while ParcelLine's references were mainly from fashion retailers with lighter parcels.

All three carriers integrate with our warehouse management system through standard interfaces, and none would require changes to our packing process or labelling. Each offers recipients a delivery-preference service to nominate a safe place or a neighbour, and each provides proof-of-delivery photographs, which our customer service team has found useful in resolving disputes.

7. Recommendation
ParcelLine offers the lowest delivery cost, met our service requirements in the trial and reduces customer contacts through its tracking app. We recommend awarding the standard parcel contract to ParcelLine for 12 months from 1 October 2026, saving up to £76,000 a year against the alternatives.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "On-time delivery was above 95% for all three carriers during the trial" -- Table 1 shows ParcelLine's on-time delivery was 93.1%, below the 95% requirement. The claim (and the recommendation that ParcelLine 'met our service requirements') misreads the table; ParcelLine's 0.9% damage rate also fails the stated 0.5% requirement.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "ParcelLine's live-tracking app clearly reduces customer contacts" -- The document states that from 1 May ParcelLine parcels alone also carried the new proactive delivery-day text message. That concurrent intervention confounds the comparison, so the lower contact rate cannot be attributed to ParcelLine's tracking app.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "ParcelLine is therefore the cheapest option, saving £2,940 a month against SwiftDrop" -- The cost comparison ignores the stated £48 cost of each damaged or lost parcel. ParcelLine's damage and loss rates (0.9% and 8 per 10,000) versus SwiftDrop's (0.4% and 3 per 10,000) imply about 231 extra problem parcels a month (about £11,100), far exceeding the £2,940 price saving; ParcelLine is likely the most expensive option overall.

REVIEW:
## Summary of the paper

The paper recommends awarding Larkspur Home's standard parcel contract to ParcelLine for 12 months from October 2026. Its case rests on three claims:
- ParcelLine has the lowest price at Larkspur's 70/30 weight mix, saving £35,000 to £76,000 a year.
- All three carriers met the 95% on-time threshold in a randomised two-month trial.
- ParcelLine's tracking app halved "where is my order?" contacts.

## Verdict

The trial is well designed and the price arithmetic is correct. But ParcelLine **failed two of the four requirements the paper sets out**, and the paper says it met them. Once the paper's own £48 cost per damaged or lost parcel is included, ParcelLine becomes **the most expensive option**, not the cheapest. The customer-contact advantage is also confounded with a text-message trial run only on ParcelLine. On this evidence the recommendation should change.

## 1. ParcelLine fails the stated requirements

Section 2 sets the requirements: **on-time delivery of at least 95%** and a **damage rate below 0.5%**.

| | On-time (min. 95%) | Damage (max. 0.5%) |
|---|---|---|
| SwiftDrop | 96.2% ✓ | 0.4% ✓ |
| ParcelLine | **93.1% ✗** | **0.9% ✗** |
| Meridian | 97.5% ✓ | 0.3% ✓ |

Section 3 says on-time delivery "was above 95% for all three carriers." Table 1 shows ParcelLine at 93.1%. The recommendation says ParcelLine "met our service requirements." It met neither of the two measured performance requirements, and its damage rate is more than double the limit.

These are not small-sample artefacts. With about 5,000 parcels per carrier, damage counts of roughly 45 for ParcelLine against 20 for SwiftDrop and 15 for Meridian are clearly different. So is the 3-point gap in on-time delivery.

The lost-parcel figures are a different matter. At about 5,000 parcels each, they rest on only one to four lost parcels per carrier, so they shouldn't be given much weight.

## 2. Including damage and loss reverses the cost ranking

The price comparison is correct as far as it goes: £3.55, £3.48 and £3.63 per parcel, and the monthly totals check out. But the paper also says each damaged or lost parcel costs **£48**, and then leaves that cost out of the comparison. Adding it in, at 42,000 parcels a month:

| | Delivery cost/month | Damaged + lost parcels/month | Cost at £48 | **Total/month** | **Total/year** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SwiftDrop | £149,100 | ≈ 181 | £8,669 | **£157,769** | **≈ £1.893m** |
| Meridian | £152,460 | ≈ 134 | £6,451 | **£158,911** | **≈ £1.907m** |
| ParcelLine | £146,160 | ≈ 412 | £19,757 | **£165,917** | **≈ £1.991m** |

This treats the damage and loss rates as separate, and adds them together.

On total cost, **ParcelLine is about £98,000 a year dearer than SwiftDrop, and about £84,000 dearer than Meridian.** The claimed saving of "up to £76,000" becomes a loss of similar size. This is before counting the one-star reviews that the paper says damaged items cause.

One check could narrow the gap: compensation from the carrier. If a carrier reimburses lost or damaged goods, the effective £48 is lower. But ParcelLine's terms would have to be far more generous for that to close an £84,000 to £98,000 gap.

## 3. The customer-contact advantage is confounded

Section 5 credits ParcelLine's tracking app with reducing "where is my order?" contacts to 6 per 1,000 parcels, against 11 and 10 for the others. But the same section notes that **from 1 May, only ParcelLine parcels carried the new proactive delivery-day text**. That covers half the trial. The text alone could explain the difference, and the trial can't separate the two.

The comparison also won't carry forward. The text is being rolled out to all carriers, so any advantage it gave ParcelLine will disappear. At most the saving is £670 a month, which is small next to the damage costs above. The statement that the app "clearly reduces customer contacts" should be withdrawn, unless the April data, before the text was introduced, show a similar gap.

## 4. Peak-season risk

- **The trial ran in April and May**, outside peak season. The contract starts on 1 October, so peak trading falls in the first three months.
- **ParcelLine's references are mainly from fashion retailers with lighter parcels.** SwiftDrop and Meridian have handled peak volumes for retailers of similar size.
- **Damage probably comes mostly from the heavier 2–10 kg items**, such as lamps, mirrors and small furniture. If so, ParcelLine's high damage rate may reflect how it handles exactly the items Larkspur ships that are least like a fashion retailer's.

The paper could check this by splitting damage by weight band, which the trial data should allow.

## 5. What is sound

- **The trial design is strong.** Parcels were randomly allocated by the warehouse management system, and it measured on-time delivery, customer-reported damage and losses. That makes the head-to-head comparison fair, as the author says.
- **The price calculations are correct.** The 70/30 weighting, the monthly totals and the differences of £2,940 and £6,300 all check out.
- **Clear requirements and a cost per incident.** Stating the requirements up front, and putting a figure on the cost of damage, is good practice. It is exactly what makes the full comparison possible.
- **Candour about the text trial.** Disclosing that the text message ran only on ParcelLine parcels is honest, even though the paper then draws the wrong conclusion from it.
- **The other comparisons are useful.** Integration, collection times and proof-of-delivery photos are relevant points of comparison.

## 6. The author's description vs. the document

- **"All three carriers cleared our 95% on-time threshold."** ParcelLine scored 93.1%.
- **"Not trading reliability for price."** ParcelLine also has more than double the damage rate the paper allows.
- **"Saving between about £35,000 and £76,000."** Including damage and loss at the paper's own £48, ParcelLine costs about £84,000 to £98,000 more a year.
- **"Shows the value of its live-tracking app."** The contact data are confounded with the text trial.

## 7. What the evidence supports

- **SwiftDrop** has the lowest total cost, meets every requirement, has peak-season experience and offers a 12-month term. On this evidence it is the strongest choice.
- **Meridian** has the best service figures at about £14,000 a year more than SwiftDrop, but requires a 24-month term. It's a reasonable alternative if Larkspur values reliability and is happy to commit for longer.
- **ParcelLine** shouldn't be chosen on this evidence. It fails two stated requirements and costs the most in total.

## Recommendations for revising the paper

1. Correct the on-time statement, and add a compliance table showing each carrier against each requirement.
2. Add the total-cost comparison, including damage and loss at £48 per incident, adjusted for any carrier compensation.
3. Remove the claim about the tracking app. Re-run the contact comparison on April data only, before the text was introduced.
4. Split damage by weight band, and address peak-season experience.
5. Revise the recommendation, probably to SwiftDrop, with Meridian as the alternative if reliability is prioritised over contract flexibility.

If it would help, I can draft a revised Sections 4 and 7 with the total-cost table and an updated recommendation.
